KEY MESSAGE 1...

In the mid/upper-levels, an increasingly progressive wave train 
exists over the northern half of the U.S. and into Canada, with a 
cyclonic gyre meandering over eastern Canada. Several series of 
shorter-wave perturbations continue to propagate through the 
northern-stream jetlet stretching across the Medicine Line/49th 
parallel, with a compact, shortwave trough evident on water-vapor 
imagery over Lake Superior. This fast-moving feature will continue 
to propagate southeastward and emerge over the northern Appalachian 
Mountains by this afternoon, which will aid in maintaining the belt 
of northwesterly flow aloft. The 10/00Z objectively analyzed UA 
charts also observed geopotential height tendencies of +05 to +09 
dam across the region, due to the presence of a low-amplitude, 
shortwave ridge migrating ahead of the upstream trough. The net 
increase in geopotential heights will yield even warmer temperatures 
compared to yesterday, with highs peaking about 5-10 degrees above 
seasonal norms, depending on the locale.

At the surface, the synoptic cold front associated with the 
shortwave trough emerging over the Great Lakes extended southward 
into northern MI, WI, and across the Corn Belt; and this front is 
expected to continue moving east and eventually stall to the north 
of the I-70 corridor this afternoon. As this occurs, a pre-frontal 
surface trough will cross through the CWA and shift winds towards 
the west in congruence with the southward shift of the surface 
anticyclone. Dewpoints were lowered from the NBM to match current 
observations and through tonight; however, modest moistening of the 
airmass will occur as winds transition to the west. This will yield 
RH minima about 5-10 percent higher than yesterday across the 
lowlands and mountains despite the warmer temperatures. Localized 
wind gusts in the 10-20 mph range are forecast across the higher 
terrain this afternoon, while winds remain anemic otherwise across 
the CWA. Therefore, fire weather concerns are low today. Persistence 
forecasting has been applied to Wednesday, with similar sensible 
weather conditions expected compared to today.

By Wednesday night, an amplifying shortwave trough will be digging 
into the Middle Mississippi River Valley, while an inverted trough 
on the western tranche of the cyclonic gyre dives southward across 
the Great Lakes region. These two features are forecast to phase 
following a large-scale wave break event over the Pacific Coast, 
thereby governing the erosion of the cyclonic gyre as the meridional 
waveguide widens substantially from multiple shortwave troughs 
emanating from the higher latitudes. The leading shortwave trough 
is forecast to remain open as it ejects over the CWA early Thursday, 
with moist, isentropic ascent increasing accordingly in congruence 
with frontogenesis and the deepening of the surface low as it moves 
eastward across the Ohio River Valley. PoPs will increase quickly as 
early as late Wednesday night as WAA strengthens ahead of the cold 
front, with widespread rainfall forecast to envelope the CWA during 
the day Thursday. A modest isallobaric response from the deepening 
surface low beneath the amplifying trough will also translate into 
blustery wind gusts post-FROPA, and high temperatures for Thursday 
have trended slightly cooler from the previous forecasts. Additional 
adjustments to the high temperatures Thursday may be required, as a 
non-diurnal temperature curve appears likely (i.e., the temperature 
will fall throughout the morning and afternoon). However, this will 
be contingent on the frontal timing. Irrespective of the frontal 
timing and temperatures, only plain rain is forecast area-wide 
Thursday before a transition to a rain-snow mix occurs across the 
northeastern mountains late Thursday night into Friday.

The phasing into a large-scale trough should be completed by Friday 
night, with the closed, mid-level cyclone rotating east of the CWA 
and northwesterly flow advecting in aloft. The resultant NVA will 
begin to entrain the lower theta surfaces with drier air, with PoPs 
gradually dwindling across the lowland throughout the day Friday and 
beyond. Farther east into the mountains, the upslope regime will 
maintain the potential for at least light snowfall to continue 
throughout the day Friday into Saturday. Orographically-enhanced 
snowfall will gradually wane by Saturday night due to drier air 
aloft entraining the columns as the core of the system moves off 
into the Canadian Maritimes. Total QPF for this event appears to 
range between 0.50"-1.00", with locally higher liquid-equivalency 
amounts possible, which is a slight uptick from the previous 
assessments. Light accumulations of snow are forecast across the 
mountains for this event, and while a brief transition to snow may 
occur across portions of the lowlands on the backside of this 
system, no snow accumulations are expected for those areas. Dry and
